subject: Problem Converting to Log Odds in Model

messages.author: 34c298f03949f42c
messages.subject: Problem Converting to Log Odds in Model
parts:
Hey everyone,

This is my first post here, so I apologize for any style blunders I may have committed.

I have a hierarchical model of clinical trials where a binary outcome was recorded. This model is similar to the example in Bayesian Data Analysis on meta-analyses. For each trial, I have the number of subjects and the number of successful treatments. Each trial is modeled a binomial distribution. The probability of success is then converted to log odds and described by a normal distribution. When I compute the log-odds conversion, I receive the following warning in R for line 15 of the model:
Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) contains a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
 You must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.

I would appreciate any help that anyone can provide on addressing this warning. I have included the model as an attachment to this message.

Thanks,
Daniel Chamberlain

messages.author: 1d05bb6779340540
messages.subject: Re: Problem Converting to Log Odds in Model
parts:
I don't think you can assign the same variable twice:

transformed parameters {
  theta[j] <- logit(p[j]); // conversion to log odds. This line throws the warning.

 and here

model{
  theta[j] ~ normal(mu,sigma);

I'm not familiar with odds models. But usually you specify the model fit theta_hat in the transformed block and then 'sample' the 'error' (actually update the log prob.) in the model block, e.g. theta ~ normal(theta_hat, sigma). Following this 'design pattern' should solve your problem.

Cheers,
J

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problem Converting to Log Odds in Model
parts:
There are a lot of problems with that model.

But multiple assignment isn't one of them. To start,

> theta[j] ~ normal(mu,sigma);

isn't an assignment in Stan, it's equivalent to

increment_log_prob(normal_log(theta[j], mu, sigma));

modulo constant terms.

The problem is that you want to do this the other way around.
Declare the parameter thetato be unconstrained,

parameters {
vector[J] theta;
...

and then you can do this:

transformed parameters {
vector<lower=0,upper=1>[J] p;
for (j in 1:J)
p[j] <- inv_logit(theta[j]);

Note the loop. You can't just have a dangling p[j] or theta[j] without
defining j.

But you can vectorize the model, writing

theta ~ normal(mu, sigma);

instead of

for (n in 1:N)
theta[j] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Finally, what you really want to do is just use the logit-scaled
parameter version of binomial directly

y ~ binomial_logit(n, theta);

Again, this is vectorized. You can't just have dangling j.

Then if you really need the p values and don't want to compute them on the
outside, define them as generated quantities,

generated quantities {
vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] p;
for (n in 1:N)
p[n] <- inv_logit(theta[n]);
}

- Bob
